web_review.quote: On a conjoint analysis of Exb P1, P2 and deposition of Syed Abdul Nabi, it could be safely concluded that the Respondent is in absolute ownership and continuous possession of the suit property for the last about one century. Their title is valid.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately captures the affirmative title basis independently of adverse possession. The Supreme Court relied on the reported protected-monuments register, city survey records and Syed Abdul Nabi's testimony, while finding no concrete evidence substantiating the appellants' competing ownership claim. The four slots identify relevant evidentiary considerations without converting them into automatically sufficient conditions. OPEN_TEXT is essential because the court's conjoint analysis requires substantive assessment of the records, testimony and opposition. The conclusion is supported as a possible result of that evaluation, and the judgment expressly reached the affirmative title finding. The rule appropriately distinguishes party assertions, reported documents, testimony, trial-court findings, High Court affirmance and Supreme Court evaluation. Its scope limits prevent mere possession, monument protection or management from becoming conclusive ownership evidence. The opposing Wakf account is preserved as an asserted historical case rejected for insufficient substantiation, not established factual falsity. The burden policy appropriately avoids inventing a comprehensive allocation of title burdens. Independent authentication, credibility assessment, statutory interpretation and combined evidentiary weighing are expressly unimplemented. The rule is acceptable only as this source-specific, non-mechanical research translation.

web_review.quote: The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved. So are the aspects of earlier title of Appellant or the point of time of disposition.
web_review.reason: The rule faithfully identifies three specific deficiencies recorded by the Supreme Court: insufficient specific pleading and proof of exclusive possession with the requisite intention, the appellant's alleged earlier title, and the relevant point of disposition. The source uses the word 'disposition'; the rule's description of a supposed dispossession must remain a contextual interpretation of that language, not a finding that dispossession occurred. ALL is justified because the conclusion merely records the conjunction of the three deficiencies expressly identified together in the judgment. It does not purport to reproduce the complete legal test for adverse possession. The conclusion is appropriately limited to recorded pleading and evidentiary gaps and does not independently determine the ultimate adverse-possession ground. No exception is necessary for this descriptive classification. The burden policy is supported by the court's express requirement that the person asserting adverse possession clearly plead and establish the necessary facts. The rule correctly avoids deriving factual nonexistence from non-proof or inventing an actual date. Independent assessment of pleadings and the full substantive legal standard remains unimplemented.

web_review.quote: The pleas on title and adverse possession are mutually inconsistent and the latter does not begin to operate until the former is renounced.
web_review.reason: The rule faithfully preserves the distinction between an asserted original-title basis and an alternative claim to acquire title adversely to another owner. The judgment records both theories and recounts precedent establishing their inconsistency and the significance of renouncing the original-title basis. ALL appropriately requires both theories to be asserted by the same claimant concerning the same property before concluding that the inconsistency and renunciation question is triggered. The conclusion correctly stops at identifying that legal tension. It does not automatically invalidate every alternative pleading, presume that renunciation never occurred or establish when adverse possession began. The reported contractual circumstances of Mohan Lal are appropriately excluded from the facts of these suits. The precedent quotations are treated as the target judgment's account rather than independently examined authorities. The empty exception slots are acceptable because the renunciation qualification is expressly preserved in the scope limits and the conclusion is deliberately narrow. NOT_COVERED correctly avoids inventing a burden allocation for proving renunciation. Actual renunciation, its timing and its legal effectiveness remain unimplemented.

web_review.quote: Since he is trying to defeat the rights of true owner, it is for him to clearly plead and establish all facts necessary to establish his adverse possession.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately reconstructs the governing adverse-possession analysis and the limited basis for rejecting the alternative ground in this case. The Supreme Court requires legally hostile possession denying the true owner's title, adequate continuity, publicity and extent, and specific pleading and proof of relevant facts. It identifies physical exclusive possession and animus possidendi as especially important and treats adverse possession as a mixed question of fact and law. The recorded failures concerning exclusionary possession, intention, earlier opposing title and the relevant point of disposition support the court's conclusion that the alternative ground was unsustainable. OPEN_TEXT is appropriate because the requirements cannot be reduced to a mechanical checklist. The R3 deficiency classification supplies the directly decisive record gaps; the R4 inconsistency classification supplies a separate legal consideration rather than an independent automatic bar. The conclusion does not depend on proving that renunciation was absent. The empty exception slots do not omit a decisive exception within the rule's stated scope, because the contextual qualifications are expressly included. The burden policy directly reflects the Supreme Court's assignment of pleading and proof responsibility to the adverse-possession claimant. The rule properly refrains from generalizing the 12-year period in the reported Mohan Lal discussion. Assessment of hostile possession, relevant dates, duration, statutory requirements and any renunciation remains a substantive unimplemented evaluation.

web_review.quote: The High Court need not have stated that the first respondent is entitled to the relief even on the basis of adverse possession.
web_review.reason: The rule faithfully expresses the limited independence of the two title theories demonstrated by the judgment. The Supreme Court reached an affirmative title conclusion on its conjoint assessment of documentary evidence and testimony, while rejecting the High Court's additional reliance on adverse possession. ALL appropriately combines an independently established affirmative title ground with an unsuccessful alternative adverse-possession ground to produce only the proposition that failure of the alternative does not itself invalidate affirmative title. Neither antecedent is sufficient alone for the exact relational conclusion. The rule does not use the ultimate dismissal of the appeals as a premise, infer title from deficiencies in adverse-possession pleading, or treat the failed alternative theory as affirmative proof of ownership. The relevant subjects and properties must remain consistent across the two antecedents. The scope limits correctly preserve the different procedural findings and reserve independent appellate requirements. No separate exception is missing for this limited logical inference. NOT_COVERED appropriately avoids inventing an appellate burden rule. Because R2 and R5 are OPEN_TEXT evaluations, their substantive execution remains unimplemented; R6 cannot bypass them or mechanically generate the Supreme Court's disposition.

S5.quote: As we have already found, Respondent obtained title under the provisions of cite10†Ancient Monuments Act . The element of Respondent's possession of the suit property to the exclusion of the Appellant with the animus to possess it is not specifically pleaded and proved. So are the aspects of earlier title of Appellant or the point of time of disposition. Consequently, the alternative plea of adverse possession by Respondent is unsustainable. High Court ought not have found the case in their favour on this ground.
